Use only the content of Table 1 to build the structure. Do not pull data values from text outside the table, and do not add your own totals or statistics.

1) Identify columns
- Read the header from left to right and list every explicit data column header in `columns`.
- If there is a multi-level header (a top label spanning several subcolumns), treat only the lowest-level headers as data columns. Form each `column_label` by combining the group and leaf text with a separator (e.g., "Group: Leaf").
- If the leftmost label column has its own heading, include that heading in `columns`, but never make data cells for that column. Its entries are captured as `row_label`.
- Every `column_label` used in any cell must appear exactly once in `columns`. Do not invent extra column names such as overall totals or combined groups unless they are explicitly printed as headers.

2) Distinguish row_group from row_label
- Scan down the first column and separate:
  • Section or category headings, which visually group several subsequent rows (often spanning columns or styled differently).
  • Regular data rows, which align with values in data columns.
- Use the text of each section heading as `row_group` for all data rows it groups. The specific item name on each row becomes `row_label`.
- If a data row does not clearly belong to any section, set `row_group` = null.
- When a section heading itself has data in the same row, represent that line with `row_group` equal to the heading text and `row_label` = null.
- Do not swap these roles: `row_group` is the broader category; `row_label` is the individual item inside that category.

3) Creating cells
- A cell corresponds to a single non-empty intersection of one data row and one data column.
- For every visible entry in the body of the table (numbers, text, percentages, symbols), create exactly one cell object with `row_group`, `row_label`, `column_label`, and `value`.
- Copy the value exactly as printed, including punctuation, spacing, parentheses, ranges, units, percent signs, plus/minus signs, and textual markers such as "N/A" or dashes when they appear as values.
- Treat printed zeros as real values and include them.
- Do not create cells for blank entries, and never infer or calculate values that are not shown.

4) Avoid missing and extra cells
- Work row by row. For each data row, scan across all data columns and ensure that every non-empty table entry is represented once in `cells`.
- Do not create cells on rows that are purely header or category lines and contain no data values.
- Do not move values between categories: a value appearing under a specific section heading and row name must remain associated with that same `row_group` and `row_label`.
- Do not add overall or combined cells (for example, totals or summary statistics) unless they are explicitly present as table entries with their own row and column positions.

5) Uniqueness and consistency
- Each combination of (`row_group`, `row_label`, `column_label`) must appear at most once in `cells`; do not duplicate a value for the same position.
- Use the table wording exactly for `row_group`, `row_label`, and `column_label`, preserving spelling, capitalization, and symbols so that repeated sections and columns match perfectly.
